You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Bank of America Global Fund Manager Survey: Cash Falls to 3.6%, Semiconductor Crowding at 82%, Three Contrarian Clues Amid Extreme Optimism

TEXT:
1. Odds have worsened, but the trend has not reversed. Interviewed fund managers have reduced their cash ratio from 4.1% to 3.6%. The Bank of America Bull & Bear Indicator has risen to 9.4, both now within historical sell territory. At the same time, global equity overweight has reached a net 42%, and US equity overweight has reached a net 24%. Fundamentals may still materialize, but incremental buying has decreased, so any data below expectations will more easily trigger portfolio adjustments.
2. Macro consensus is close to an ideal mix, but real risks come from internal portfolio conflicts. 54% of respondents expect a 'no landing' global economy, with a net 21% expecting an economic upturn; meanwhile, a net 4% expect inflation to fall, and 83% believe the Federal Reserve will not raise rates before the US midterm elections. Markets are essentially betting on a combination of strong growth, falling inflation, and loose policy. If just one of these conditions falls short, industrials, banks, and high beta assets will be repriced.
3. The main risk of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has shifted from "is there demand" to "who bears the financing and return pressure". 82% of respondents see long global semiconductors as the most crowded trade, while 45% list the AI bubble as the biggest tail risk; but 61% still do not believe hyperscale cloud providers will cut capital expenditures. More notably, 48% think related capex is most likely to trigger the next systemic credit event. The risk focus is now shifting from the income statement to the balance sheet.
4. Extremely underweighted defensive assets offer better contrarian odds. The position in consumer staples fell to a net -32% underweight, 2.0 standard deviations below the historical average; UK equities are a net -37% underweight, 1.8 standard deviations low; energy stocks are a net -20% underweight, 1.4 standard deviations low. These may not enter trend trades immediately, but if the Federal Reserve turns hawkish, growth peaks, or AI capex expectations waver, their lower crowding makes them more capable for positioning upside.
5. Portfolio allocations should shift from "betting on direction" to "betting on conditions". The base scenario can still retain US equities, healthcare, and high-quality growth, but indiscriminate chasing of semiconductors is not advisable. Should short-term rates turn hawkish, focus first on consumer staples and gold; if economic momentum peaks, the relative win rate of duration assets, UK equities, and high dividend strategies increases. Going forward, four variables should continuously be monitored—cash, capex, inflation, and credit spreads—and allocations adjusted according to whether they simultaneously worsen.
To avoid losing contact, feel free to follow the backup account, which will also update daily.

Good news has been fully priced in by the current positioning—a key contradiction risk assets need to be wary of. The July survey shows strong consensus around growth, rate cuts, and AI capital expenditure, but low cash, crowded semiconductors, and underweighted defensive assets are tightening the margin for further chasing.
What really happened in the survey: Optimism isn’t the issue; positioning ahead of fundamentals is
Bank of America’s July global fund manager survey covered 210 respondents managing some $555 billion in assets, including global questions answered by 181 respondents with around $484 billion in assets under management. The survey period was from July 2nd to 9th, with respondents’ weighted average investment horizon only 7.1 months; thus, it is more a tactical position map for global institutions rather than a long-term value judgment for the next 3-5 years.
The most striking shift on this map is sentiment, cash, and risk exposure all moving in the direction of greater optimism. The composite sentiment index rose from 6.0 to 7.2, the highest since February 2026; global equities positioning rose to a net 42% overweight; US equities to a net 24% overweight, not only above last month’s 17%, but also the highest since December 2024. The cash position held by fund managers decreased from 4.1% to 3.6%, also back to the lowest level since February 2026.
